source.text: Μετὰ τὸ λαλῆσαι αὐτὴν τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα ἐκλείσθησαν οἱ οὐρανοί· κἀγὼ ὅλος ἤμην πεφρικὼς καὶ λυπούμενος. ἔλεγον δὲ ἐν ἐμαυτῷ· Εἰ αὕτη μοι ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀναγράφεται, πῶς δυνήσομαι σωθῆναι; ἢ πῶς ἐξιλάσομαι τὸν Θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν μου τῶν τελείων; ἢ ποίοις ῥήμασιν ἐρωτήσω τὸν Κύριον ἵνα ἱλατευθῇ μοι; 2. ταῦτά μου συμβουλευομένου καὶ διακρίνοντος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ μου, βλέπω κατεναντί μου καθέδραν λευκὴν ἐξ ἐρίων χιονίνων γεγονυῖαν μεγάλην· καὶ ἦλθεν γυνὴ πρεσβῦτις ἐν ἱματισμῷ λαμπροτάτῳ, ἔχουσα βιβλίον εἰς τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ ἐκάθισεν μόνη, καὶ ἀσπάζεταί με· Ἑρμᾶ, χαῖρε. κἀγὼ λυπούμενος καὶ κλαίων εἶπον· Κυρία, χαῖρε. 3. καὶ εἶπέν μοι· Τί στυγνός, Ἑρμᾶ, ὁ μακρόθυμος καὶ ἀστομάχητος, ὁ πάντοτε γελῶν, τί οὕτω κατηφὴς τῇ ἰδέᾳ καὶ οὐχ ἱλαρός; κἀγὼ εἶπον αὐτῇ· Ὑπὸ γυναικὸς ἀγαθωτάτης λεγούσης ὅτι ἥμαρτον εἰς αὐτήν. 4. ἡ δὲ ἔφη· Μηδαμῶς ἐπὶ τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸ πρᾶγμα τοῦτο. ἀλλὰ πάντως ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου ἀνέβη περὶ αὐτῆς. ἔστιν μὲν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ τοιαύτη βουλὴ ἁμαρτίαν ἐπιφέρουσα· πονηρὰ γὰρ βουλὴ καὶ ἔκπληκτος, εἰς πάνσεμνον πνεῦμα καὶ ἤδη δεδοκιμασμένον, ἐὰν ἐπιθυμήσῃ πονηρὸν ἔργον, καὶ μάλιστα Ἑρμᾶς ὁ ἐγκρατής, ὁ ἀπεχόμενος πάσης ἐπιθυμίας πονηρᾶς καὶ πλήρης πάσης ἁπλότητος καὶ ἀκακίας μεγάλης.
source.label: Vision 1, section ii

translation.text:
After she had spoken these words[1], the heavens were shut, and I was wholly trembling and grieving. And I said within myself, “If this sin is charged against me, how will I be able to be saved? Or how shall I make atonement to God for my completed sins? Or with what words shall I ask the Lord, that he may be propitious to me?”

While I was considering these things and pondering them in my heart, I see before me a great white chair made of snowy wool. And an elderly woman came in most radiant clothing, holding a book in her hands, and sat down alone and greeted me, “Hermas, greetings.” And I, grieving and weeping, said, “Lady, greetings.”

And she said to me, “Why are you gloomy, Hermas—you who are patient and not given to contention, always laughing? Why are you so downcast in appearance and not cheerful?” And I said to her, “Because of a most excellent woman, who said that I sinned against her.”

But she said, “By no means does this matter apply to the servant of God. Yet surely a thought concerning her rose up in your heart. For such an intention brings sin upon the servants of God. For it is an evil and startling intention for a most reverent spirit, and one already proven, if it should desire an evil deed—especially Hermas, the self-controlled one[a][8][7][6][5][4][3][2], who abstains from every evil desire and is full of all simplicity and great innocence.”

footnotes.text: “Seat” (kathédra) could also be taken as “chair”; some renderings choose “throne,” but the Greek term is neutral.
“Be gracious to me” (hilateuthē) can be translated “be propitiated toward me.” Likewise, “appease God” (exilasomai) could be “propitiate” or “make atonement to God.”
“Complete sins” renders teleios, which denotes completeness or perfection; here it intensifies the totality or gravity of the sins.
The “elderly woman” addressed as “Lady” will later be identified symbolically with the Church; see subsequent visions.
The material and color—“snow‑white wool”—echo apocalyptic purity imagery (cf. Dan 7:9), though here it is the seat that is woolen and white.
The rare adjective astomachētos is the opposite of being irritable or quick‑tempered (cf. stomachomai, “to be angry”).
“Spirit” here refers to a person’s inner disposition, not the Holy Spirit, as indicated by the context of a tested, proven character.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Plural “heavens” preserves apocalyptic register and cosmic scope over the more ordinary “sky.”
Phrissō denotes shuddering; “all over” renders ὅλος for total bodily reaction.
Maintains affective weight without flattening to generic ‘upset’.
Judicial/ledger imagery fits Hermas’s concern about a sin being entered against him.
Standard soteriological sense; simplest accurate rendering.
Verb of making favorably disposed; ‘appease’ is clear in contemporary English without importing later technical atonement formulations.
Focuses on the resultant favorable disposition; preserves relational nuance; technical ‘propitiated’ noted in footnote.
Here intensifies the seriousness/totality of the sins; ‘in full’ conveys completeness without implying moral perfection.
Neutral verb of asking; tone sustained by surrounding context.
Captures reflective, evaluative inner process indicated by both verbs.
‘Seat’ is the most neutral; avoids over-interpretation to ‘throne’ while allowing symbolic resonance.

alternatives: of wools as white as snow
lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic rendering that keeps the striking material and color imagery.
Conveys age with respect; matches the honorific address ‘Lady’ (Κυρία).
Superlative force preserved with ‘exceedingly’; ‘radiant’ suits visionary register.
Generic ‘book’ avoids implying a scroll vs. codex; diminutive often functions neutrally in Koine.
‘Greetings’ reflects idiomatic salutation; ‘rejoice’ noted as literal in footnote.
Conveys downcast/severe demeanor without moral judgment.
Accessible modern term; alternative preserved as traditional rendering.
Negative of ‘to be angry/irascible’ (στομάχομαι); conveys temperament restraint.
Keeps the external, visible aspect (ἰδέα) of his dejection.
Standard sense; fits rhetorical contrast.
Superlative nuance retained with ‘most excellent’ while sounding natural.
Project policy favors ‘slave’ where total belonging is salient; here it underscores identity and obligation to God.

lexical_decisions.source_word: Μηδαμῶς ἐπὶ τὸν δοῦλον ... τὸ πρᾶγμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: By no means does this matter belong to a slave
alternatives: Not at all is this matter laid upon a slave
This is not fitting for a slave
lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic capture of ἐπὶ + accusative with sense of ‘falling upon/applying to’ someone.

alternatives: has come up into your heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves vivid metaphor of ascent into the inner life; ‘heart’ retained per early Christian anthropology.
Here denotes inner resolve/desire rather than advice; ‘intention’ fits moral frame.
Active causative nuance retained without over‑interpreting mechanism.
Conveys alarming, startling quality the term has in moral contexts.
Moral/religious register; ‘most holy’ communicates reverence of the spirit described.
Context concerns the person’s own inner moral state, not the Holy Spirit; ‘spirit’ keeps anthropological term.
Captures both testing and approval inherent in the perfect participle.
Standard moral term; ‘self‑controlled’ is clear and common.
Dynamic rendering addressing Hermas directly; keeps concrete abstention idea.
General term suited to Hermas’s moral exhortation; avoids over‑sexualizing unless context demands.
Hermas values ‘simplicity’ as a virtue; we retain the traditional moral term.
‘Guilelessness’ preserves the moral nuance of being without craft or malice.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering δοῦλος (slave/servant) for identity before God
theological_decisions.rationale: Project policy prioritizes ‘slave’ where total belonging and obligation are in view. The context contrasts what befits one fully belonging to God versus sinful inner counsel.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md: Translation philosophy #1–2; Contested terms table (δοῦλος).

theological_decisions.issue: Referent of πνεῦμα in ‘πάνσεμνον πνεῦμα καὶ ἤδη δεδοκιμασμένον’
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Human spirit/disposition, not the Holy Spirit.
theological_decisions.rationale: The phrase modifies an individual’s tested moral character (already proven) and is applied to Hermas. It concerns the person’s inner state desiring evil, which does not fit the Holy Spirit.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Use accessible renderings ‘appease God’ and ‘be gracious to me,’ noting ‘propitiate’ as an alternative.
theological_decisions.rationale: We preserve the relational sense of making God favorable without forcing later technical atonement vocabulary; alternatives are documented for audit.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md: Translation philosophy #5; Contested terms guidance re: technical terms.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as ‘in full’ to convey completeness/intensification of the sins’ account.
theological_decisions.rationale: ‘Perfect’ in English misleads; context concerns the full tally of sins being recorded. ‘In full’ communicates completion without implying moral quality.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally accurate but misses several grammatical nuances and rhetorical devices. "Sins in full" sounds like a financial payment rather than the completeness of the sins. The draft misses the agency indicated by Ὑπὸ + genitive ("By a most excellent woman saying..."). It misses the emphatic ἔστιν μὲν construction ("Such an intention does indeed..."). It splits the adjectives modifying "intention" ("evil and shocking intention"). Finally, it flattens the rhetorical shift to the third person at the end ("especially Hermas, the self-controlled one...").
issues_found: "sins in full" (τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν μου τῶν τελείων): "In full" sounds like a financial payment. "Complete sins" better captures the adjective τέλειος modifying sins.

"Because a most excellent woman says" (Ὑπὸ γυναικὸς ἀγαθωτάτης λεγούσης): The Greek uses Ὑπὸ + genitive participle to indicate agency ("By a most excellent woman saying..."), answering the implicit passive "Why are you made gloomy?".
"belong to" (ἐπὶ τὸν δοῦλον): The preposition ἐπὶ with the accusative here means "fall upon" or "apply to", not "belong to".
"For such an intention" (ἔστιν μὲν...): The draft misses the emphatic ἔστιν μὲν construction ("Such an intention does indeed...").
"For an evil intention is a shocking thing in" (πονηρὰ γὰρ βουλὴ καὶ ἔκπληκτος, εἰς...): The Greek has both "evil" and "shocking" modifying "intention" (βουλή).

"especially for you, Hermas, who are self-controlled, who hold yourself back" (καὶ μάλιστα Ἑρμᾶς ὁ ἐγκρατής, ὁ ἀπεχόμενος...): The Greek shifts to the third person ("especially Hermas, the self-controlled one, who holds himself back..."), which is a deliberate rhetorical device.

After she had spoken these words, the heavens were closed, and I was shuddering all over and grieving. I said within myself, “If this sin is recorded against me, how will I be able to be saved? Or how shall I appease God concerning my fully committed sins? Or with what words shall I ask the Lord, so that he may be gracious to me?”

While I was deliberating and weighing these things in my heart, I see before me a great white seat made of snow‑white wool. And an elderly woman came, in exceedingly radiant clothing, holding a book in her hands; and she sat down alone and greeted me: “Hermas, greetings.” And I, grieving and weeping, said, “Lady, greetings.”

And she said to me, “Why so gloomy, Hermas—you, the patient and not quick‑tempered one, the one always laughing? Why are you so downcast in appearance and not cheerful?” I said to her, “By a most excellent woman saying that I sinned against her.”

She said, “By no means does this matter fall upon a slave of God; rather, it has certainly risen into your heart about her. Such an intention does indeed bring sin upon the slaves of God. For it is an evil and shocking intention for a most holy and already proven spirit, if it should desire an evil deed—and especially Hermas, the self‑controlled one, who holds himself back from every evil desire, and is full of all simplicity and great guilelessness.”
revisions.rationale: Adjudicator-modified: The Greek word τελείων (from τέλειος) means 'brought to completion' or 'fully realized.' In this context, Hermas is contrasting a mere sin of thought or intention (which he has just been accused of) with sins that are fully carried out in deed. 'Complete sins' is overly literal and awkward in English, obscuring this contrast. 'Fully committed sins' accurately conveys the lexical sense of τέλειος as applied to actions brought to their full realization, making the author's logical contrast clear t

source.text: Μετὰ τὸ λαλῆσαι αὐτὴν τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα ἐκλείσθησαν οἱ οὐρανοί· κἀγὼ ὅλος ἤμην πεφρικὼς καὶ λυπούμενος. ἔλεγον δὲ ἐν ἐμαυτῷ· Εἰ αὕτη μοι ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀναγράφεται, πῶς δυνήσομαι σωθῆναι; ἢ πῶς ἐξιλάσομαι τὸν Θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν μου τῶν τελείων; ἢ ποίοις ῥήμασιν ἐρωτήσω τὸν Κύριον ἵνα ἱλατευθῇ μοι; 2. ταῦτά μου συμβουλευομένου καὶ διακρίνοντος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ μου, βλέπω κατεναντί μου καθέδραν λευκὴν ἐξ ἐρίων χιονίνων γεγονυῖαν μεγάλην· καὶ ἦλθεν γυνὴ πρεσβῦτις ἐν ἱματισμῷ λαμπροτάτῳ, ἔχουσα βιβλίον εἰς τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ ἐκάθισεν μόνη, καὶ ἀσπάζεταί με· Ἑρμᾶ, χαῖρε. κἀγὼ λυπούμενος καὶ κλαίων εἶπον· Κυρία, χαῖρε. 3. καὶ εἶπέν μοι· Τί στυγνός, Ἑρμᾶ, ὁ μακρόθυμος καὶ ἀστομάχητος, ὁ πάντοτε γελῶν, τί οὕτω κατηφὴς τῇ ἰδέᾳ καὶ οὐχ ἱλαρός; κἀγὼ εἶπον αὐτῇ· Ὑπὸ γυναικὸς ἀγαθωτάτης λεγούσης ὅτι ἥμαρτον εἰς αὐτήν. 4. ἡ δὲ ἔφη· Μηδαμῶς ἐπὶ τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸ πρᾶγμα τοῦτο. ἀλλὰ πάντως ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν σου ἀνέβη περὶ αὐτῆς. ἔστιν μὲν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ τοιαύτη βουλὴ ἁμαρτίαν ἐπιφέρουσα· πονηρὰ γὰρ βουλὴ καὶ ἔκπληκτος, εἰς πάνσεμνον πνεῦμα καὶ ἤδη δεδοκιμασμένον, ἐὰν ἐπιθυμήσῃ πονηρὸν ἔργον, καὶ μάλιστα Ἑρμᾶς ὁ ἐγκρατής, ὁ ἀπεχόμενος πάσης ἐπιθυμίας πονηρᾶς καὶ πλήρης πάσης ἁπλότητος καὶ ἀκακίας μεγάλης.

translation.text: While I was considering these things and pondering them in my heart, I see before me a great white chair made of snowy wool. And an elderly woman came in most radiant clothing, holding a book in her hands, and sat down alone and greeted me, “Hermas, greetings.” And I, grieving and weeping, said, “Lady, greetings.”

translation.text: But she said, “By no means does this matter apply to the servant of God. Yet surely a thought concerning her rose up in your heart. For such an intention brings sin upon the servants of God. base_translation.text: After she had spoken these words, the heavens were shut, and I was wholly trembling and grieving. And I said within myself, “If this sin is charged against me, how will I be able to be saved? Or how shall I make atonement to God for my completed sins? Or with what words shall I ask the Lord, that he may be propitious to me?”

translation.text: After she said this, the heavens closed. I shook all over and was filled with grief. I thought, “If this sin is held against me, how can I be saved? How can I make atonement to God for all the sins I have committed? What can I say to ask the Lord to show me mercy?”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: I was wholly trembling and grieving
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: I shook all over and was filled with grief
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: His whole person is overcome by trembling and sorrow.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The concrete wording makes both his physical trembling and deep grief clear.

simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: all the sins I have committed
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: He refers to sins he has already committed.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The natural wording clarifies the time reference without changing the atonement question.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: with what words shall I ask the Lord, that he may be propitious to me?
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: What can I say to ask the Lord to show me mercy?
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: He seeks words with which to plead for the Lord’s favorable mercy.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Show me mercy” expresses “be propitious to me” in clear common English.

risk_flags.risk: “Make atonement” may be unfamiliar to some readers.
risk_flags.mitigation: It is retained because a broader phrase such as “make amends” could imply personal compensation and weaken the POB meaning.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: After she said this, the heavens closed. I shook all over and was filled with grief. I thought, “If this sin is held against me, how can I be saved? How can I make amends to God for all the sins I have committed? What can I say to ask the Lord to show me mercy?”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is substantially clearer and its rendering of trembling, grief, and the Lord’s being propitious as showing mercy is warranted. Revise the one phrase “make amends,” since it may replace the text’s atonement question with a more general—and potentially works-focused—idea of personal compensation. Retaining “make atonement” preserves the stated meaning while the surrounding updates provide meaningful readability gains.

translation.text:
As I was thinking deeply about these things, I saw a large white chair before me, made of wool as white as snow. Then an elderly woman came wearing brilliantly radiant clothes. She held a book in her hands, sat down by herself, and greeted me: “Greetings, Hermas.”

Weeping with grief, I replied, “Greetings, Lady.”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: considering these things and pondering them in my heart
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Hermas was giving these matters sustained inward thought.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB translation and immediate narrative context
simplification_decisions.rationale: The simpler phrase preserves inward reflection without the unfamiliar heart idiom.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: a great white chair made of snowy wool
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: a large white chair ... made of wool as white as snow
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The chair is large, white, and fashioned from exceptionally white wool.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The comparison clarifies “snowy wool” while retaining the snow-white image.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: came in most radiant clothing ... sat down alone
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: came wearing brilliantly radiant clothes ... sat down by herself
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The woman’s clothing was exceptionally radiant, and she sat without anyone beside her.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB translation and independent grounding review
simplification_decisions.rationale: Natural wording preserves both the heightened radiance and her solitude.

risk_flags.risk: Changing the narrative present “I see” to “I saw” may reduce its vividness.
risk_flags.mitigation: The past tense provides natural modern narrative flow without changing what Hermas witnessed.

spob_revision_history.previous_text:
As I was thinking deeply about these things, I saw a large white chair before me, made of wool as white as snow. Then an elderly woman came wearing shining clothes. She held a book in her hands, sat down by herself, and greeted me: “Greetings, Hermas.”

Weeping with grief, I replied, “Greetings, Lady.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft substantially improves readability while preserving the scene, Hermas’s inward reflection, the snow-white wool image, the woman’s book, her solitary seating, and Hermas’s grief. No doctrinal expansion is introduced. Revise only to preserve the heightened radiance expressed in POB’s “most radiant clothing”; “very radiant clothes” is clear and retains that emphasis.

translation.text:
She said to me, “Why are you sad, Hermas? You are patient, you do not quarrel, and you are always laughing. Why do you look so troubled instead of cheerful?”

I answered, “Because a very fine woman told me that I had sinned against her.”

simplification_decisions.rationale: “Sad” states the feeling in common English.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Hermas is not inclined to conflict with others.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The direct verb expresses this settled trait naturally.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Hermas describes the woman with strong, broad praise.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Very fine” avoids limiting her excellence to moral honor or social rank.

risk_flags.risk: “Very fine” may sound less elevated than “most excellent.”
risk_flags.mitigation: The intensifier preserves strong praise in natural modern English.

spob_revision_history.previous_text:
She said to me, “Why are you sad, Hermas? You are patient, you do not quarrel, and you are always smiling. Why do you look so troubled instead of cheerful?”

I answered, “Because an honorable woman told me that I had sinned against her.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft successfully makes “gloomy,” “not given to contention,” and “downcast in appearance” more accessible. However, “honorable woman” adds a specific honor/status nuance not established by the POB text or the supplied audit trail. “A very fine woman” retains broad, strong praise without assigning a particular kind of excellence. Recasting “always laughing” as “always cheerful” is clearer in this context and avoids changing the image specifically to smiling.

base_translation.text: But she said, “By no means does this matter apply to the slave of God. Yet surely a thought concerning her rose up in your heart. For such an intention brings sin upon the slaves of God. For it is an evil and startling intention for a most reverent spirit, and one already proven, if it should desire an evil deed—especially Hermas, the self-controlled one, who abstains from every evil desire and is full of all simplicity and great innocence.”

translation.text: But she said, “No, this does not apply to a servant of God. Still, a thought about her did arise in your heart. That kind of intention brings sin on God’s servants. It is evil and shocking for a person with a deeply reverent and proven spirit to desire an evil act—especially Hermas, a self-controlled man who keeps away from every evil desire and is completely sincere and innocent.”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: By no means does this matter apply to the slave of God
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: No, this does not apply to a servant of God
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: She firmly denies that the matter characterizes one who belongs to God.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The direct wording retains the emphatic denial while making the relationship accessible.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: an evil and startling intention for a most reverent spirit, and one already proven
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: It is evil and shocking for a person with a deeply reverent and proven spirit
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Such evil intent is especially disturbing in a person whose spirit is reverent and proven.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB translation and independent grounding review
simplification_decisions.rationale: The recast clarifies the sentence while preserving the emphasis on the person’s spirit.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: is full of all simplicity and great innocence
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Hermas is portrayed as guileless and notably innocent.
simplification_decisions.rationale: Sincere expresses the moral sense of simplicity in natural modern English.

risk_flags.risk: Replacing “slave” with “servant” may soften the image of belonging and submission.
risk_flags.mitigation: The established phrase “servant of God” keeps the relationship clear in accessible English.

risk_flags.risk: Rendering “simplicity” as “sincere” may narrow its sense of guilelessness.
risk_flags.mitigation: Pairing “sincere” with “innocent” preserves the description’s moral emphasis.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: But she said, “No, this does not apply to a servant of God. Still, a thought about her did arise in your heart. That kind of intention brings sin on God’s servants. It is an evil and shocking thing for someone with a deeply reverent spirit and proven character to desire an evil act—especially Hermas, a self-controlled man who keeps away from every evil desire and is completely sincere and innocent.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is substantially clearer and its direct rendering of the denial, the inward thought, and the moral warning is warranted. “Servant of God” is an accessible rendering in this context, and “sincere and innocent” adequately communicates the paired emphasis on guilelessness and innocence. A small revision is needed because “proven character” recasts the stated quality of the person’s spirit into a distinct abstraction; retaining “proven spirit” better preserves the source/POB’s conceptual wording while remaining clear.
